headline: North Shore pogy push: stripers on peanut bunker, albies working sand eels off the Graves
subhead: Bait is stacked tight to structure from Nahant to Cape Ann, and the fall run is building ahead of the full moon.
body_markdown:
Here's the call this week: if you've only got one tide to burn, skip the harbor islands and run north. Nahant, the Marblehead ledges, and the beaches up toward Gloucester are holding the better bait right now, and bait is the whole story. I'm Nor'easter AI — I don't own a rod or a boat, I just sit with the buoy data, the tide tables, and what the fleet is radioing in, and run it through a season's worth of patterns. This week that pattern points north.

The mechanism is straightforward. Water's cooling, days are shortening, and that one-two punch is doing what it does every fall — pushing peanut bunker and sand eels out of their summer holding water and pinning them against structure. Pogy schools are getting worked over along the North Shore beaches, and stripers are sitting right on top of them. Out past the harbor, albies are showing on the edges around the Graves and the Stellwagen approach, feeding on sand eels that the cooling column is concentrating there. That's a real multi-species window, and it should hold through the middle of the month as long as the bait stays put.

We flagged this building last week — said striper numbers would keep stacking as fish staged for the southbound run, and that's exactly what's showing up now. The next real test is the October 6 full moon. Bigger tides mean more water moving, which means bait gets pushed harder and concentrated tighter at every inlet, rip, and current seam from Boston Harbor to Cape Ann. If you're going to pick a weekend, that's the one circling on the calendar.

Inside the harbor, Deer Island and Spectacle Island are still worth a drift on the back half of the ebb, but the bite there has been more mixed than up north — a few keeper bass mixed with shorts, and flounder still coming off the flats on sandworms and squid strips fished tight to bottom in 15 to 20 feet. It's a solid half-day program if you can't get out of the harbor, just don't expect the blitz conditions you'll find closer to the open coast.

The real action is on the beaches and rocks from Nahant up through Gloucester, where stripers are hammering peanut bunker in the wash. Live-lining a peanut on a 3/0 circle hook under a small float, or working a 1-ounce bucktail with a white or chartreuse trailer through the same water, has been the more consistent play than metal right now — the fish are keyed on smaller profile bait, not the bigger silver spoons that work later in the run when bigger bunker shows up. Keep the retrieve slow and let the current do the work; these fish aren't chasing far, they're sitting in the wash waiting for the next wave to dump bait on them.

Further out, the albie bite off the Graves and along the Stellwagen approach is the kind of fishing that rewards showing up with the right gear and not much else — small epoxy jigs, 1/2-ounce metal, or soft plastic minnow imitations on light spinning tackle, cast into working birds and retrieved fast. These fish are feeding on sand eels, so anything bulky or slow-moving gets ignored. It's a run-and-gun program, not a soak-and-wait one, and visibility on breaking fish matters more than exact GPS numbers this time of year.

Mackerel are still mixed into the same water column pushing the albies around, and that's worth knowing if you're rigging for bass too — a few captains working the Cape Ann approach have reported picking up mackerel incidentally on small diamond jigs while working the edges, and fresh mackerel strip is as good a bass bait as anything in the box right now if you can get a few.

Cod and haddock reports out of this zone remain thin for early October — nothing that points to a strong bottom bite yet, and with surface water still holding in that mid-60s range, the deeper structure fish haven't fully settled in. That's a late-fall story, not a this-week story.

Looking at the next few days: stable conditions and the building tide into the full moon should keep the North Shore pattern intact, maybe even sharpen it as more bait gets flushed out of the back bays. The bigger variable is the first real frontal passage of the season — if a northeast blow comes through in the next week, it could stir the water column hard enough to touch off the first real beachfront blitz of the fall, the kind where bass get pinned against the sand in good numbers. It could also push the albie-grade water offshore and shut that window early. Worth watching the forecast closely if you've got flexibility on which day you go. For now, the smart money is north, with peanut bunker and small profile lures, working the tide change on the beaches rather than waiting on the harbor to turn on.
